A ball’s fate depends only on which piston fires while it is on the three-ball platform, not on its number.  What matters is the position (left = L, middle = M, right = R) the ball occupies when the piston fires.  

If the ball is in position L:
  • piston 1 fires ⇒ it is ejected (win) (1∕3)
  • piston 2 or 3 fires ⇒ it is released, not ejected (lose) (2∕3)
 → P(win | L) = 1∕3.

If the ball is in position M:
  • piston 2 fires ⇒ ejected (1∕3)
  • piston 1 or 3 fires ⇒ it moves to L (2∕3) then has the 1∕3 chance above.
 → P(win | M) = 1∕3 + (2∕3)(1∕3) = 5∕9.

If the ball is in position R:
  • piston 3 fires ⇒ ejected (1∕3)
  • piston 1 fires ⇒ it moves to M (1∕3)
  • piston 2 fires ⇒ it moves to L (1∕3)
 → P(win | R) = 1∕3 + (1∕3)(5∕9) + (1∕3)(1∕3) = 17∕27 ≈ 0.6296.

At the very start the balls 1, 2, 3 occupy L, M, R respectively, so their winning chances are:
  Ball 1 = 1∕3 ≈ 0.3333
  Ball 2 = 5∕9 ≈ 0.5556
  Ball 3 = 17∕27 ≈ 0.6296.

Later balls sometimes enter in M and sometimes in R; the long-run entry probabilities make their average chance 0.6, never exceeding ball 3’s 0.6296.  Therefore no other ball can beat ball 3’s probability of being ejected.

Let d0 … d12 be the 13 digits (hyphens ignored).  The check digit rule is the same as ISBN-13 except the alternating weights are 1 and an unknown w (1<w<10):
   (Σ_{p=0}^{11}  w_p·d_p  + d12) ≡ 0  (mod 10)
with w_p = 1 for even p, w for odd p.

Because two adjacent columns i and i+1 were swapped in every row (with 3≤i≤10), the stored sum differs from the correct sum by
   Δ = (w_i−w_{i+1})(d_{i+1}−d_i).
If i is odd, w_i−w_{i+1}=w−1; if i is even, w_i−w_{i+1}=1−w.
Therefore each row gives a congruence
   (S_even + d12) + w·S_odd  + (w_i−w_{i+1})(d_{i+1}−d_i) ≡ 0  (mod 10),
which simplifies to
   a·w + c ≡ 0 (mod 10)
with known a,c once i is fixed.

For every candidate i (3…10) we computed these ten congruences.  All candidates except i=9 produced an immediate contradiction (either a=0,c≠0 for some row or no common w in 1…9).

For i = 9 (columns 9 and 10 swapped):
   The ten equations reduce to
      {2w≡4, 8w≡6, 3w≡1, w≡7, 6w≡2, 6w≡2, 3w≡1, 7w≡9, 4w≡8, 7w≡9} (mod 10),
   whose unique simultaneous solution in 1…9 is w = 7.

Hence the only weighting factor that validates all ten rows after swapping columns 9 and 10 is w = 7.

Let (a,b,c) be the numbers of coins in the three boxes; a+b+c=30 and some pair differs by exactly 6.  The largest number any box can hold is therefore 24 (it occurs in the distribution 0,6,24).

Bob guesses g coins for every box (if he uses different numbers, the host can reorder the boxes to pair Bob’s largest guess with the smallest box, so using one common guess cannot be worse).

Bob’s gain for a distribution (a,b,c) is S(g)=min(g,a)+min(g,b)+min(g,c).

• If Bob chooses g≥24, then every box contains ≤24 coins, so min(g,a)=a, min(g,b)=b, min(g,c)=c.  Consequently S(g)=a+b+c=30, no matter how the host distributes the coins.

• If Bob chooses any smaller g, the host can use the arrangement (0,6,24), which satisfies the game’s rules.  That gives Bob only 0+min(g,6)+min(g,24)=g+6 coins (<30 for g<24).

Thus the maximum guaranteed number of coins is achieved by taking g=24 (or any larger number), yielding a sure 30 coins.  Each coin is worth $1,000, so the guaranteed money is 30×1,000.
